## Conclusion

Cities with severe, persistent central-area congestion and a transit network able to absorb diverted trips should adopt it; cities without both should not, and the question as posed hides that split. The implemented schemes reduced traffic volumes and delays and raised substantial net revenue, and none of the three reviewed here has been repealed [1][2][3]. The strongest objection is that a cordon simply relocates congestion to the streets outside it, which would make the measured reduction an accounting artefact rather than a gain — the monitoring data do not support that reading, though they do show the effect is real at the boundary [1][2]. Adopt, in other words, is conditional on the transit alternative and on a design that manages the cordon edge.

## Key findings

- London's 2003 charge reduced traffic in the zone by roughly 15 percent in its first year and cut delays by about 30 percent [1].
- Stockholm's 2006 trial reduced zone traffic by around 20 percent, and a referendum held after the trial converted it into a permanent scheme [2].
- New York's 2025 scheme reduced vehicle entries to the Manhattan central business district by about 8 percent in its first quarter, with transit ridership rising over the same period [3].
- Support for the Stockholm scheme was substantially higher after residents had experienced the trial than before it, and both the traffic effect and that support held five years on [2][5].
- The standard theory of congestion pricing treats the charge as a correction to a price that is otherwise set below marginal social cost, which is why scheme design rather than the decision to price carries most of the practical difficulty [4].
- Both the London and Stockholm schemes direct net revenue to transit capital programmes, and the durability of each appears to track visible reinvestment [1][2].

## The strongest counterargument

The serious objection is that a cordon charge does not reduce driving, it moves it. Traffic that would have crossed the boundary reroutes around it, congestion appears on the ring of streets just outside the charged zone, and the headline reduction inside the cordon is then a measurement boundary rather than a change in behaviour. Stated at its strongest, the claim is that these schemes buy an improvement for the centre at the expense of the neighbourhoods on its edge, and that those neighbourhoods were never asked.

What the objection gets right is that the boundary effect is real and measurable: rerouting at the cordon edge is documented in the monitoring, and it is the standard argument for corridor or distance-based pricing over a simple cordon [1][2]. What would have to hold for the conclusion to flip is that the diverted traffic roughly cancels the reduction inside — and it does not. London's monitoring records reduced vehicle kilometres across an area wider than the zone itself [1], and Stockholm's zone reduction was accompanied by a measured shift onto transit rather than purely onto other roads [2]. The objection therefore constrains scheme design, which is why the recommendation above is conditioned on it, but it does not overturn the case for pricing.

## Evidence from implementations

London's 2003 charge reduced traffic in the zone by roughly 15 percent in its first year and cut delays by about 30 percent, effects that persisted through the monitoring period [1]. Stockholm's 2006 trial reduced zone traffic by around 20 percent; the referendum that followed converted the trial into a permanent scheme, and support was substantially higher after residents had experienced it than before [2].

New York's 2025 scheme reduced vehicle entries to the Manhattan central business district by about 8 percent in its first quarter, with transit ridership rising over the same period [3]. The scheme is too new for anything beyond first-quarter effects to be read from it.

The Stockholm case is the only one with a long enough record to say whether first-year effects hold. Reviewed five years after introduction, the traffic reduction persisted and public acceptability was higher than at any point before the trial [5]. That is the closest thing in this evidence to a durability result, and it is a single city.

## Design and revenue

Scheme design matters more than the decision to price. In the standard treatment the charge corrects a price set below marginal social cost, and almost all of the practical difficulty sits in how the charge is levied rather than in whether to levy one [4]. Cordon schemes are simpler to administer but create sharp boundary effects at the cordon edge, where drivers reroute to avoid the charge and push traffic onto adjacent streets [2]. Corridor and distance-based schemes avoid that but require denser sensing infrastructure [4].

Collection cost is the other design variable that decides whether a scheme is worth running. London's original camera-based enforcement consumed a substantial share of gross revenue, and the net figure is the only one worth quoting when comparing schemes [1]. Stockholm's automated system carries a lower collection overhead, at the price of infrastructure that has to be built before any revenue arrives [2].

Revenue is substantial and, in every scheme reviewed, hypothecated. Both the London and Stockholm schemes direct net revenue to transit capital programmes [1][2], and durability appears to depend on that reinvestment being visible: Stockholm's referendum passed after residents had seen both the traffic effect and the spending [2].
